order.readMe: Optional item field next to `transition` / `transitionDuration`, deciding which of the two clips gives ground to create the overlap the transition crosses. "Next over previous" (the default) slides THIS clip earlier by transitionDuration, onto the tail of the clip before it; that clip does not move and the timeline gets shorter by the overlap. "Previous over next" leaves this clip exactly where it is and slides the PREVIOUS clip later instead, so its tail lands on this clip's head; the timeline keeps its full length and a gap of the overlap opens in front of the clip that moved (together with anything already welded to it by its own transition, which travels with it). The transition itself renders identically either way — same frames, same direction, same duration, same `overlapIn`. Only where the clips sit changes, so every render path follows it for free.

easings.readMe: `kind` names the field that IS the curve. `bezier` → `cubicBezier` = [x1, y1, x2, y2] in CSS cubic-bezier order, restated ready to paste in `css`. `sampled` → `samples` = the curve at t = 0, 0.01 … 1 (101 points; values outside 0..1 are real overshoot, not an error) — as CSS that is `linear(<samples, comma-separated>)`. `gsap` names the ease the editor plays. A `sampled` entry may also carry `cubicBezier` with `bezierIsApproximate`: that is the closest single cubic (the handles the graph editor draws) and `bezierMaxError` is how far off it runs — use the samples wherever the curve has to match. Everything here is reusable as-is outside the app.

keyframe.description: Values for a keyframe's `easing` (keyframes[].easing, propertyKeyframes tracks) and for transitions. An easing set on a key shapes the segment AFTER it.

curves.note: The key carries its own curve as `bezier: [x1, y1, x2, y2]` (CSS cubic-bezier order, y may overshoot 0..1). Without it the key falls back to Smooth.
Steps: the value is held until the next key instead of being interpolated.

motionTemplate.description: Values for a motion template's ease fields (motionParams). Each template's own fields[].options lists the subset it offers; these are the curves behind those values.

keyframeExpressions.readMe: Set item.propertyKeyframeFx = { [trackKey]: { type, params } } on any item whose propertyKeyframes has that track. Applies to numeric tracks only (not colors or shape paths). elastic/bounce RESHAPE each move (every keyframe transition is replayed through a profile normalized to that segment, so the layer overshoots or lands into the key as one continuous motion) and therefore supersede that track's per-key easing — mix back toward it with the amp/Strength param. glide SOFTENS the keyed motion (easing included): an all-positive filter — fast response + slow tail carrying weight% of each move — so a move lands soft and keeps creeping on in its own direction, never past the key and never back; `presets` lists the tuned landings as ready param sets. wiggle is additive and leaves the base motion intact. custom evaluates the `code` param and USES ITS RESULT as the property value (write `value` to start from the keyframed one).

types.label: Elastic
types.description: The move itself becomes springy: it launches at the key before, overshoots the target and wobbles into place.

types.label: Bounce
types.description: The move falls onto the target like a dropped ball and rebounds in decaying hops, settling on the key.

types.label: Wiggle
types.description: Continuous smooth jitter around the keyframed value, like AE wiggle().

types.label: Glide
types.description: The move lands soft and keeps sliding on in the direction it travelled, never past the key and never back. On a camera it keeps the shot alive between keys.

presets.label: Soft
presets.description: Lands soft and keeps sliding a little (Easing examples row 3)

presets.label: Floaty
presets.description: A heavier tail: a floatier, longer landing (row 4)

presets.label: Trailing
presets.description: The last quarter of the move starts 0.1 s late, like an AE null chain (row 5)

presets.label: Endless
presets.description: A long, light tail that never visibly stops before the next move (row 6)

types.label: Custom
types.description: Write your own expression. The result becomes the property value.

customLanguage.readMe: A safe AE-flavoured expression language (interpreted, never eval'd). One expression, no statements or assignment. Numbers only; the result is the property value. A syntax error or a non-numeric result silently leaves the keyframed value untouched.

variables.value: the property's keyframed value at this moment
variables.time: seconds since the start of the clip
variables.frame: whole frames since the start of the clip
variables.progress: 0 at the clip start, 1 at its end

functions.math: abs ceil floor round sqrt exp log sin cos tan asin acos atan atan2 pow min max sign hypot — bare or under Math.*
functions.linear: linear(t, tMin, tMax, a, b) or linear(t, a, b) — remap with clamping
functions.ease: ease / easeIn / easeOut, same signature as linear
functions.wiggle: wiggle(freq, amount, octaves?) — deterministic smooth jitter around `value`
functions.random: random() / random(max) / random(min, max) — deterministic per frame and call site
functions.loops: loopOut(type?, numKeyframes?) repeats this track's own animation past its last key; loopIn(…) does the same before the first. type is "cycle" (default), "pingpong", "offset" (each pass stacks on the previous) or "continue" (no repeat — keep going at the end velocity). numKeyframes counts keys of the looped segment back from the edge, 0 = the whole track. loopOutDuration(type, seconds) / loopInDuration(type, seconds) take seconds instead.
functions.track: valueAtTime(t) — this property's keyframed value at another clip-local time; numKeys — how many keys this track has
functions.glide: glide(fast?, slow?, weight?, delay?) — inertia without spring-back: this track's own keyframed motion through a filter with only positive weights — a fast response (time constant `fast` s, default 0.10) plus a slow tail (`slow` s, default 0.6) carrying `weight` (0–1, default 0.25) of every move, optionally `delay`ed. The move lands soft and keeps creeping on in the direction it travelled: never past the key, never back. Presets: glide(0.10, 0.6, 0.25) soft, glide(0.10, 1.0, 0.40) floaty, glide(0.10, 0.45, 0.25, 0.10) 75/25, glide(0.10, 2.0, 0.14) never stops. Same call on X and Y glides a 2D path; on camera tracks it keeps a shot alive between keys (key one framing per shot, let glide do the drift).

customLanguage.layers: layer("Layer Name").<trackKey> reads another layer's animated property at the same instant; thisLayer.<trackKey> reads this layer's. thisComp.layer("…") also works. Only layers that share a frame with this clip can be named, the name is the layer's custom name (or text content / clip name). A REAL property the target does not animate falls back to its static value, but a name that is not a property at all is an error rather than a silent 0. Referencing a layer that itself references back stops after two hops.
customLanguage.sequences: A sequence or grid layer hides its own timeline. Chain .layer() to read into it: layer("My Sequence").layer("Inner").opacity. The inner clock follows the container's placement, trim and speed, so the value is what that inner layer really shows at this instant; chain again for nested containers (two levels deep).

paths.readMe: One anchor record covers every bezier path in the editor: a shape layer's `shapePath`, a `line` outline, each Layer Mask's `path`, an item's `motionPath` and a camera's `cameraPath`. `hIn`/`hOut` are the cubic-bezier control handles stored as OFFSETS FROM THEIR OWN ANCHOR, not absolute control points — the segment A→B is the cubic A → A+A.hOut → B+B.hIn → B. A missing or zero-length handle is a CORNER. Auto-smoothing runs ONLY inside the interactive editor (when a human adds or drags a point); loading, saving, the preview, WebCodecs export and /render-onserver all draw the stored handles verbatim, so a path written as bare x/y points renders as a straight-line polygon rather than a curve. Always write both handles AND `manual: true` on every anchor.

anchor.x: anchor position in this path's space (see `spaces`)
anchor.y: anchor position in this path's space
anchor.z: world-space paths only (motionPath / cameraPath); omit in unit-box space
anchor.hIn: handle for the segment ARRIVING at this anchor, as an offset from it: { x, y, (z) }
anchor.hOut: handle for the segment LEAVING this anchor, as an offset from it: { x, y, (z) }
anchor.manual: true = hand-shaped, the auto-tangent pass must leave these handles alone. Set it on every generated anchor, or the next point a user adds in the UI re-smooths the whole path.

spaces.unitBox: shapePath, line outlines and Layer Mask paths. Fractions of the element's own box, centred on it: -0.5 is the left/TOP edge and +0.5 the right/BOTTOM, so +y points DOWN. Anchors AND handles are clamped to ±8 on load; anchors outside ±0.5 are legal (the render plate grows to fit). 2D — no z.
spaces.world: motionPath and cameraPath. Composition pixels, origin at the comp centre: x right, y UP, z toward the viewer. Unclamped; every anchor and handle carries z. The two share this space exactly, so points transfer between a layer path and a camera path literally.

tangents.smooth: The Catmull-Rom tangent the editor itself writes: hOut = (P[next] - P[prev]) / 6 and hIn = -hOut, componentwise. A CLOSED path wraps (the neighbour before the first anchor is the last). On an OPEN path the first anchor uses hOut = (P[1] - P[0]) / 3 and the last hIn = -(P[last] - P[last-1]) / 3.
tangents.corner: hIn and hOut both zero — { "x": 0, "y": 0 } (plus "z": 0 in world space).
tangents.cusp: hIn and hOut pointing in directions that are not opposite: curvature on both sides, but a visible break in the tangent.
tangents.circularArc: A quarter-arc needs handles of 0.5522847498307936 x radius laid PERPENDICULAR to the anchor's radius, following the winding — 0.2761 in the unit box, where the radius is 0.5. That is the Circle preset. Longer handles bulge the arc (Squircle uses 1.34x), shorter ones flatten it toward a polygon.

paths.presetsReadMe: Ready-to-paste outlines in unit-box space with handles already resolved. They scale with the shape's Width/Height, so the points never change with size. `shapePresets` are closed (filled shapes, and the valid starting points for a Layer Mask); `linePresets` are open (stroked lines — `closed: false`). `pointCount` matters for a keyframed morph: every key of a `shapePath` or `msk:<mid>:path` track must hold the SAME number of points, so pick presets whose counts match, or resample.

params.label: Reference Layer
params.note: The clip's source picture is measured (a video: its thumbnail). The layer can sit anywhere on the timeline and its channel can stay hidden.

params.label: Texture Layer
params.title: Another layer in this project whose picture fills this layer's silhouette
params.note: The texture must be a layer on another channel that overlaps this clip in time. It is used as drawn — position, scale, keyframes, effects — and while the effect is on it is hidden on its own and shows only inside this layer.

layer.name: Mockup Frame
notes: Draws a device chassis AROUND the layer and re-seats the layer’s own pixels in its screen. The chassis is PATH GEOMETRY re-drawn at the isolate’s live pixel size, so a camera push finds more detail instead of a softer edge.

mfDevice picks the chassis: browser, iphone17air, pixel, ipad13, mbp16, mba15, imac24, xdr, iphone17, imacSpaceGrey, watch. mfFinish picks a colour from that device’s own list and is ignored by the two artwork frames, which are single-finish.

mfSizeMode 0 fits the whole chassis inside the layer box so nothing clips. 1 matches the chassis SCREEN to the layer box, which keeps the artwork at its original size and lets the chassis overflow — that is the case that wants mfFit around 70.
Rotating a chassis with mfOrient carries its screen with it, exactly as real hardware does; mfMediaUpright (default on) counter-rotates the artwork and swaps the cover/contain box.
mfVariant / mfTheme / mfUrl apply to the browser chassis only (safari, chrome, arc, minimal).

layer.name: Build Depth Map
notes: Estimates a monocular depth map (Depth Anything V2 small, in a worker) ONCE and stores it on the layer as a small base64 PNG, so it travels with the project and re-renders identically in exports.
Renders NOTHING on its own. It is the source 3D Depth and Depth Scan read; adding either of those adds this automatically.
dmInvert flips which end of the range is near — needed when a depth map made by another tool uses the opposite convention.

layer.name: Depth Scan
notes: A LiDAR-style slice THROUGH DEPTH, not a screen wipe: every pixel whose depth is within scnWidth of the moving threshold lights up, so the contour crawls over the subject's surface instead of marching across the frame.

scnColorMode picks how the slice is coloured. 0 RGB Split draws three bands at phase-split / phase / phase+split (the reference look). 1 Flat Color draws one band in scnColor. 2 Gradient draws one band widened to width+split with scnRamp laid across it, so scnSplit still means "how far the colours spread through depth".

The sweep is a pure function of clip time: phase = scnPhase + scnSpeed x seconds, wrapped. scnEase 1 (Hold Ends) applies a closed-form remap so it crawls at the extremes, rather than integrating per frame — a rendered frame must not depend on how many frames preceded it.
scnBorder rejects the depth CLIFF at the subject silhouette. At 0 the silhouette becomes a permanent outline that never moves, which is what makes the effect read as a filter rather than a scan.
scnView 1/2 (Depth Map / Original) RENDER — they are diagnostics you can leave on by accident.

layer.name: Fresnel Rim
notes: On a 3D model layer: rim light from the model's own normals (1 − n·v) inside its 3D pass, with its own even halo; it turns with the model and lights edges inside the outline. No depth map is needed there, and the frPhase…frBgDim fields are ignored.

On an image or video layer: needs Build Depth Map. Only EDGES glow — wherever depth falls away behind a pixel — fading inward over frRimPx (px of a 1080-tall frame); frEdgeMin is the smallest depth drop that counts. Like Depth Scan, a depth window (frWindow ± frFeather) around frPhase picks which edges light up, swept by frSpeed with frEase; frWidth / frSoftness are ignored there.
frHalo 0 skips the halo pass; frAmount 0 is an exact bypass.

layer.name: Motion Trail
notes: Three methods, chosen by trailMethod. 0 Frame Echo replays a ring of past PLATES, so it is the only one that carries motion from inside the footage; 1 Trail Buffer keeps one accumulator and erodes it trailTaper px per frame for a continuous comet; 2 Transform Repeats re-draws the current plate at past poses with no history at all.
Every method carries the FINISHED layer look (glow, defocus, overlay chain, tiles) and follows the real motion path, parenting and follow rigs included.
Frame Echo and Transform Repeats share trailCount/trailSpacing/trailDecay and the drift set (max 32 repeats); Trail Buffer ignores those and uses trailPersist/trailTaper instead.

Frame Echo and Trail Buffer are temporal: a seek rebuilds them from reprojected poses, so a scrubbed frame is usable but can differ slightly from a sequential export on footage whose pixels move internally.
Spacing is counted in 30fps timeline frames and may be fractional: small values give a continuous smear, large ones give stepped ghosts.

trailScale is a SIGNED per-repeat delta about the layer's own centre: 0 neutral, negative tapers to a comet, positive grows the tail. Projects written by 9.6.35 stored it as an 80–120 multiplier and are migrated on load.

layer.name: Region Distort
notes: Rescales only what is inside the band; the rest of the layer slides but keeps its shape.
Region geometry is PERCENT OF THE LAYER BOX with +y down, so it rides the layer through move/scale/rotate/parenting and can be keyframed like any other number.
Its sibling `bend` is the other warp from the same family and stacks on top of this one — they are separate effects because their maps share nothing.

layer.name: Bend
notes: After Effects' CC Bend It: everything outside the two axis handles stays rigid, the span between them bends around an arc and can be stretched along its own axis.
Axis geometry is PERCENT OF THE LAYER BOX with +y down, so it rides the layer through move/scale/rotate/parenting and can be keyframed like any other number.
Runs AFTER `regionDistort` when a layer carries both, so a bend arcs the already-stretched artwork.

layer.name: Corner Pin
notes: The layer box mapped onto an arbitrary quad by a projective homography, so parallel edges CONVERGE like a plane seen at an angle instead of stretching evenly — the classic way to paste artwork onto a screen, a wall or a passing van.

Corners are PERCENT OF THE LAYER BOX with +y down, in the winding UL → UR → LR → LL. The identity quad is 0,0 / 100,0 / 100,100 / 0,100 and is an exact bypass; `defaultParams` deliberately leans the top edge back so a freshly added effect shows what it does.
Every corner keyframes, which is how a pin tracks a moving surface. Corners may sit outside the box (−50…150).
Runs after `regionDistort` and `bend` when a layer carries several, so the pin lays the already-warped artwork onto the plane.
Was an Overlay Effect in 9.6.32 only; an `item.effects` entry with this id migrates into `layerEffects` on load, its 0–1 corner fractions rescaled to percent.

layer.name: Mesh Warp
notes: After Effects' Mesh Warp: a Catmull-Rom surface over a control lattice, so dragging ONE vertex moves its neighbourhood and leaves the rest of the layer alone.

The lattice is mwCols × mwRows (2–5 each) and its vertices are the numbered params mwP<i>X / mwP<i>Y, PERCENT OF THE LAYER BOX with +y down, running left→right then top→bottom. Only the first mwCols·mwRows slots are live.
Changing mwCols or mwRows RE-SEEDS the whole lattice to a regular grid (and drops any keyframe tracks on its vertices), because slot i means a different vertex at a different grid size.
Every live vertex keyframes, but its channels are published per layer rather than from the static registry — they appear in the Keyframe Builder only while the effect is on the layer.
Runs after `regionDistort` and `bend` and before `cornerPin` when a layer carries several.

layer.name: Bezier Warp
notes: After Effects' Bezier Warp: four cubic edges driving a Coons patch, so the silhouette curves smoothly instead of kinking at a vertex the way a lattice does.
Twelve points in a clockwise ring from upper left — corner, its two outgoing tangents, next corner, … — all PERCENT OF THE LAYER BOX with +y down, and all keyframable.
The identity ring (a flat box with evenly spaced tangents) is an exact bypass; `defaultParams` deliberately bends the layer into an arc so a freshly added effect shows what it does.
Runs after `regionDistort`, `bend` and `meshWarp` and before `cornerPin` when a layer carries several.

layer.name: Droste
notes: The layer falls into ITSELF, forever — Escher’s Print Gallery map. The recursion is closed form (a mod in log-polar space), so every level exists at once and depth costs nothing.
droR1/droR2 are the annulus that repeats: everything inside droR1 is the next level down. droR2 = 100 means the layer’s own edge, which is the case where nothing is cropped.

droTwist is LEVELS PER TURN. 0 is a straight frame-in-frame recursion; 1 is the classic Escher spiral. It is seamless only at WHOLE numbers — a fractional twist leaves a deliberate spiral cut on the 180° ray.

droShape morphs the nesting outline: −100 diamond, 0 circle, 100 the layer’s own RECTANGLE (the “infinite frame” look). droFit: 1 measures against the short side so a circle stays round on a wide layer.

droZoom is a continuous level offset and ONE WHOLE LEVEL IS A CLOSED LOOP — animate it by 1.0 (or set droZoomSpeed) for a seamless endless zoom. droZoomSpeed/droSpinSpeed are rates and are deliberately not keyframable; key droZoom/droSpin instead.
Runs after the free-form warps and before Corner Pin, so a recursed layer can then be laid onto a plane.

layer.name: Pryzm
notes: The layer seen through GLASS. Three kinds of glass — fluted ribs, concentric rings, a diamond lattice — are one height field with three tessellations, refracted once per wavelength.
pzRelief is how STEEP the glass is, and the shipped default sits at 1% on purpose: that look is Cell Magnify, not refraction. Turn Relief up to make it bend light, not Thickness.

pzMagnify pulls each sample toward the centre of its cell. At 100% every cell shows ONE point of the layer behind it — a mosaic of glass. It is a lens focused on the plate, which is why it is separate from IOR.
pzDisp spreads n(lambda) across pzTaps samples. Spectral is a smooth rainbow; RGB split is a hard three-tap fringe and ignores pzTaps.

FROST RIDES THE TAPS — each spectral sample is also jittered inside a disc, because a rough surface scatters each wavelength. So Frost gets smoother when you raise Taps, and a wide Frost at a low tap count shows its taps as ghosts.

pzWarpSrc: 2 drives the cell WIDTHS from the layer’s own luminance, read along the Origin crosshair. With Warp Shape on Separable the cells stay dead straight and only their spacing changes — that is the signature of this effect.
pzDrift and pzFlow are RATES (per second) and are deliberately not keyframable; key the static fields instead.
Runs after the free-form warps and before Corner Pin, in the same slot as Droste, so glass can be laid onto a plane afterwards.

layer.name: Glass
notes: The shape becomes a pane of GLASS over everything rendered BEHIND it: the layers below are refracted (with spectral dispersion), frosted, tinted and shadowed. Use it for any glass look (glassmorphism cards and buttons, liquid or frosted glass, a lens or magnifier, crystal or prism tiles) instead of faking glass with a blur, CSS backdrop-filter or a generated video.

glassPreset sets the whole look: liquid, frosted, slab, opal, magnifier, fisheye, prism, fluted, hammered, smoked, etched, gel. `{ "id": "glass", "params": { "glassPreset": "frosted" } }` is a complete pane — every other param defaults to that preset's value; send only the ones you change.
Keep the shape’s fill transparent (shapeFillColor "rgba(255,255,255,0)"): the fill draws ON TOP of the pane, so an opaque fill hides it. borderWidth / borderColor draw a rim line over it.

Glass shapes stack: one higher in the timeline refracts, frosts and shadows the glass shapes under it. The pane follows the layer transform, keyframes and 3D rotation (a tilted pane shows its thickness as side walls), fades with the layer’s opacity and respects its track matte and Layer Mask (the masked-away part shows no glass and casts no shadow).

It always works on what is behind the shape, before the shape’s own paint — its position among the other Layer Effects does not change it. % sizes (bevel, height, depth, shadow, clear border) are of the shape’s SHORTER side; frost, rim width and the pattern are px.

layer.name: Chroma Key
notes: Removes a backdrop of ANY colour, not only green: ckKeyColor is the screen colour (sample it from the footage; the editor auto-detects it as the dominant colour cluster when the effect is added). The matte then becomes the layer’s shape for every later stage — mask, glow, motion blur, track matte.

ckMethod 0 (Auto) picks the keyer from the key colour: a saturated key uses Colour Difference (Keylight-style, the key hue is rotated onto green so it handles blue, red, magenta … identically); a white or black key uses Luma; a mid grey uses 3D Colour Distance. Set 1–4 to force one.

Colour Difference: ckBalance 0–100 compares the key channel against the stronger (0) or weaker (100) of the other two — lower it (≈35) when dark skin goes semi-transparent; ckAdapt scales the expected screen level by each pixel’s brightness so a dark corner of the screen still keys. Distance keyers use ckTolerance (+ ckLumaWeight for 3D, ckChromaGuard for Luma).

ckGain / ckClipBlack / ckClipWhite are the matte levels: raise Gain or Clip Black to clear noise on the screen, lower Clip White to make the subject fully opaque. ckShrink chokes (− erodes, + grows) and ckFeather softens the matte, both in COMPOSITION px.

Spill: ckSpill clamps the key hue out of the subject (edges lit by the screen), ckSpillLuma puts the removed brightness back as grey, ckSpillTint/ckSpillTintAmt replace it with a colour instead. Off automatically for a hue-less (white/black/grey) key.

ckWrapAmt/ckWrapWidth/ckWrapColor tint the matte edge with a colour (light wrap toward the intended background — a layer effect cannot see the layers below). ckView 1/2 render the matte / a black-grey-white status view INTO THE OUTPUT: leave 0 for the result. ckAmount 0 is an exact bypass.
Runs FIRST of all per-layer stages, in place on the isolated plate, so masks, Auto Fill, DOF, Running Glow, warps, motion blur and track mattes all see the keyed silhouette.

fields.note: Bezier outline in unit-box space (±0.5, +y down) — byte-identical to item.shapePath. Every key of msk:<mid>:path MUST hold the same point count.

notes: x/y/w/h are PERCENT OF THE LAYER BOX; feather/expand/grow are COMPOSITION px.
grow is a RATE (px per second) added to expand over the clip; the Player integrates the track, so a keyed ramp accelerates rather than jumping.

The stack folds top-down in array order from an EMPTY base — but if the FIRST enabled mask is subtract or intersect the base starts FULL, so a lone Subtract cuts a hole instead of blanking the layer. A leading difference is treated as add.
Amount mixes toward "no mask": 0 leaves the layer untouched, 100 cuts fully.

A dense (per-frame / roto) msk:<mid>:path track MUST use LINEAR easing on every key — evaluatePathTrack applies the LOW key's easing, so eased per-frame keys stutter at 30–60Hz. Key positions round to 4 decimal places.
Every key of a path track must hold the SAME point count as the static path (fixed n, max 128): interpolateShapePaths clamps to the shorter list, so a count change silently truncates geometry.
The Roto panel writes tracks like this automatically: the mask box is the media's contain-fit rect and roto never keys x/y/w/h/rot, so re-crops and parent transforms ride for free.

fields.sfx: a sound id from `library` below (pick by `category` and `use`)
fields.at: "start" | "end" | "peak" (the fastest moment of its keyframed motion) | seconds from its start — default "start"
fields.align: "sync" (default: the sound's loudest moment) | "start" | "end" — which point of the sound lands on the anchor

sounds.files: The sounds are on the GreenLight sound CDN (https://dl.greenlightdash.pro/assets/sounds/v1/<file>): `build` downloads each sound a cue uses into assets/sounds/<file>, so the finished folder plays offline.
